summary: 28Mn5Ni is the Ni-bearing austenitic low-density steel Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.9C–5Ni (wt%) in the HR+CR+1023 K condition: vacuum induction melted, homogenized at 1423 K for 2.5 h, hot rolled at 1323 K to ~13 mm plate, cold rolled at room temperature to ~50% reduction (~6 mm sheet), then heat treated at 1023 K for 1 h and water quenched. It is one of three Fe–Mn–Al–C–(Ni) alloys (designated 28Mn0Ni, 28Mn5Ni, 15Mn5Ni) studied to understand how the Mn/Ni ratio controls concurrent κ-carbide/B2 precipitation and austenite recrystallization after cold deformation, and thereby the strength–ductility balance. In this condition the alloy is only partially recrystallized (~10%) and combines very high strength (YS 1289 ± 2 MPa, UTS 1537 ± 2 MPa) with moderate ductility (17 ± 1%).
composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.9C–5Ni (wt.%), determined by wet chemical analysis and emission spectroscopy as Mn 28.1 ± 0.4, Al 8.6 ± 0.04, C 0.9 ± 0.01, Ni 4.8 ± 0.04 wt.% with Fe as balance. Mn and C are austenite stabilizers that retain the FCC γ matrix at room temperature, while Al is a ferrite stabilizer that markedly lowers physical density and contributes solid-solution hardening; Ni is added because the strongly negative enthalpy of formation between Ni and Al drives precipitation of hard, Ni-rich ordered FeAl-based B2 (Fe(Ni)Al) particles during heat treatment. The three alloys of the study were chosen so that the hot-rolled B2 fraction varies from 0 (28Mn0Ni) to ~4% (28Mn5Ni) to ~12% (15Mn5Ni), isolating the effect of Ni (and of the Mn/Ni ratio) at an otherwise essentially constant Al and C level.
processing: A 30 kg ingot of each grade was produced by vacuum induction melting; the sound portion was homogenized at 1423 K for 2.5 h and then hot rolled at 1323 K to a final plate thickness of ~13 mm (condition "HR"). Samples cut from the hot-rolled plate were cold rolled at room temperature in several passes to ~50% reduction in thickness (~6 mm sheets, condition "HR+CR"); 50% was used as a common upper limit because the companion 15Mn5Ni alloy cracked beyond it. The cold-rolled sheet of this sample was then heat treated at 1023 K for 1 h followed by water quenching, and heat-treated samples are designated by their heat-treatment temperature — hence the label HR+CR+1023 K. The parent study explored a heat-treatment window of 873–1273 K (1 h + water quenching) after the same 50% cold reduction; the hot-rolling details are reported elsewhere [21].
microstructure: Partially recrystallized austenitic (γ, FCC) low-density steel with three microstructural constituents: (a) deformed, strongly banded/elongated austenite grains aligned along the rolling direction that retain stored strain, (b) fine recrystallized equiaxed austenite grains (a few μm, staying at or below the few-μm level) making up only ~10% of the structure, and (c) secondary phases, comprising thin RD-aligned prior B2 stringers plus precipitates formed during the 1023 K treatment: fine intragranular B2 (50–200 nm), coarser intergranular B2 (0.5–1.5 μm) and κ-carbides (fine and intragranular inside recrystallized grains; inhomogeneous and relatively coarser in the deformed austenite regions). The overall B2 fraction for 28Mn5Ni is near 0.1. Annealing twins are present. OIM-EBSD phase maps show a red FCC matrix with a small number of thin, mostly RD-oriented blue B2 stringers, and KAM maps show mixed green–yellow fields with blue low-misorientation patches, i.e. intermediate-to-high local misorientation compared with the fully recrystallized, low-strain Ni-free alloy. Recrystallized grain nucleation occurs mostly along γ/γ boundaries and γ/B2 interfaces.
properties: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile response (ASTM E8M flat specimens, gauge length 30 mm, width 6 mm, thickness 4–5 mm; constant cross-head speed 0.5 mm min⁻¹, initial strain rate ~3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; tests triplicated and averaged): YS (0.2% offset) = 1289 ± 2 MPa, UTS = 1537 ± 2 MPa, total tensile elongation to failure = 17 ± 1%. This is a strong but only moderately ductile condition: at the same 1023 K heat treatment the Ni-free 28Mn0Ni reaches YS 732 ± 2 MPa, UTS 1051 ± 5 MPa and TE 36 ± 2% (n = 0.30), whereas the Ni-bearing 28Mn5Ni keeps much higher strength at lower elongation. Bulk Vickers hardness (ASTM E-140-02, 30 kg/≈300 N peak load, 15 s dwell, averaged over ten measurements) was measured as part of the study; the Ni-containing alloys were consistently harder than 28Mn0Ni at every heat-treatment temperature and rose to ~500 VHN after 873 K treatment, decreasing monotonically with increasing temperature. Characterization techniques applied to this sample/study: OIM-EBSD (Zeiss Supra 55 FEG-SEM with Oxford Nordley EBSD detector, step sizes 120 nm for fine and 250 nm for coarse maps over ~100×100 µm² and ~200×200 µm² areas, three scans per sample, TSL-OIM analysis using KAM and GOS 2° criteria), XRD (Co-Kα, 45 kV, 135 mA, Rigaku), TEM (FEI TECNAI 20T G2 at 200 kV with EDAX EDS; twin-jet electropolished in mixed acid at 243 K) and post-tensile SEM fractography (Zeiss EVO 18).
mechanisms: Ni addition promotes precipitation of Ni-rich ordered B2 (FeAl-based, containing significant Mn and Ni) during heat treatment in the 973–1173 K range; this concurrent B2/κ-carbide precipitation alters the diffusion characteristics and boundary migration, delaying recovery and recrystallization of austenite so that only ~10% of the matrix is recrystallized after 1 h at 1023 K.

The second-phase population acts on recrystallization in two competing ways: coarse, elongated B2 stringers can serve as particle-stimulated nucleation (PSN) sites, whereas fine intragranular and intergranular B2/κ-carbides exert a Zener-Smith drag on boundaries; nucleation of recrystallized grains occurs predominantly along γ/γ boundaries and γ/B2 interfaces, and intragranular B2 does not pin newly recrystallized grains but may delay overall recovery, so the net effect is a marked retardation of recrystallization.

Ni-rich B2 favors increased rejection of carbon into the neighboring austenite, which facilitates κ-carbide formation in Ni-added low-density steels relative to Ni-free grades, giving the dual κ-carbide + B2 precipitation seen in 28Mn5Ni.

Heat treating in the two-phase (γ + B2) region reduces grain-boundary migration and mobility because of decreased diffusivities, so the Ni-bearing alloy keeps a fine recrystallized austenite grain size (few μm) even at 1173 K, while the B2-free 28Mn0Ni undergoes pronounced grain growth to ~40 μm.

During cold rolling the austenite deforms predominantly by planar slip, evidenced by parallel slip bands; the prior B2 stringers also deform concurrently with the matrix, undergoing dislocation accumulation, substructure development and eventual fragmentation.

The high strength of this condition follows directly from the microstructural state: a largely deformed/banded austenite matrix carrying stored strain plus dual precipitation of fine intragranular B2, coarser intergranular B2 and κ-carbides, together with only ~10% recrystallization, yields YS 1289 MPa and UTS 1537 MPa.

In the deformed austenite, dislocations cut through the fine κ-carbides and evolve into a slip-band structure with a mean slip band spacing of ~200 ± 30 nm, whereas non-shearable B2 particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion and cause early initiation of slip-band refinement — in Ni-containing low-density steels this produces inhomogeneous slip band spacing, in contrast to the homogeneous spacing of the Ni-free alloy under the same heat treatment.

The limited ductility (17%) at 1023 K is linked not only to reduced strain-hardening ability but also to crack initiation controlled by the second-phase particles; a large volume fraction of grain-boundary B2 and coarser κ-carbides limits the attainable elongation, although 28Mn5Ni still fails by ductile dimple rupture rather than by the quasi-cleavage/intergranular cracking seen in the low-Mn 15Mn5Ni alloy.
conclusions: Ni addition combined with thermomechanical processing is an effective strategy in high-Mn low-density steel: in 28Mn5Ni, dual precipitation of κ-carbides and Ni-rich B2 concurrent with an only ~10% recrystallized austenite matrix produces a much better strength level than the Ni-free 28Mn0Ni at the same heat treatment (YS 1289 vs 732 MPa, UTS 1537 vs 1051 MPa) while retaining 17% tensile elongation. Because Ni markedly retards recrystallization, the useful processing window of the Ni-containing, high-Mn alloy is wider than that of the Ni-free grade — the latter is effectively limited to about 973 K, above which recrystallization exceeds 90% and strength collapses, whereas 28Mn5Ni still offers a balanced strength–ductility combination at 1023 K and only softens to YS 900 MPa / UTS 1236 MPa with 39% elongation at 1173 K. The finding implies that the optimum thermomechanical route for such Ni-added low-density steels should aim at a microstructure containing fine nanosized precipitates plus a controlled (partial) recrystallized fraction, and that the Mn/Ni ratio governs both the B2 fraction and the extent to which recrystallization is suppressed.
unmapped: TEM-EDS point analyses of the B2 particles in 28Mn5Ni identify the phase as FeAl-based (Fe balance) but containing substantial Mn and Ni: at 973 K Mn 16.3 wt.%/14.7 at.%, Al 12.7 wt.%/23.3 at.%, Ni 24.6 wt.%/20.8 at.%; at 1173 K (particle-1) Mn 16.5/14.9, Al 14.2/25.7, Ni 26.1/21.8; at 1173 K (particle-2) Mn 15.4/13.7, Al 14.8/26.7, Ni 27.5/22.8. The B2 composition is thus nearly invariant with heat-treatment temperature in this alloy, but becomes progressively enriched in Ni as the heat-treatment temperature rises.

System-level observation relevant to the alloy family: the total B2 volume fraction comprises three types (stringer, intergranular and fine intragranular), the fine intragranular and intergranular B2 dissolving faster than the stringers as heat-treatment temperature increases; in 15Mn5Ni the B2 fraction drops from ~40% at 973 K to ~15% at 1173 K, whereas 28Mn5Ni stays near the ~0.1 level.

Mechanistic comparison drawn across the alloy family rather than specific to this sample: the pronounced concurrent B2 precipitation in Ni-containing grades delays recrystallization more strongly than κ-carbides alone; intergranular cracking along γ/B2 interfaces was documented for the low-Mn 15Mn5Ni alloy, not for 28Mn5Ni.
